title: Technological in Nature
description: Research is technological in nature under IRC Section 41 only when it relies on the physical or biological sciences, engineering or computer science.
summary: Under IRC Section 41, research is technological in nature only when its process of experimentation fundamentally relies on the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. For U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit, this test excludes social science, routine engineering, and market research, so documentation must link expenses to hard science principles.

body.text: Under IRC Section 41, research is technological in nature only when its process of experimentation fundamentally relies on the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. For U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit, this test excludes social science, routine engineering, and market research, so documentation must link expenses to hard science principles.

The Technological in Nature requirement serves as the primary statutory and regulatory gatekeeper that restricts the United States federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit—formally designated as the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41)—to investigative activities grounded in the hard sciences. Codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the statute mandates that qualified research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature. Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), promulgated by Treasury Decision 9104 (effective January 2, 2004, and applicable to taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003), defines information as technological in nature if the process of experimentation utilized to discover that information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. By anchoring eligibility to the analytical methodology employed rather than the commercial novelty or ultimate market success of the resulting product, the requirement separates creditable scientific and engineering experimentation from non-creditable business risk, aesthetic design, routine production, and social science inquiry.

Crucially, satisfying the Technological in Nature mandate does not require a taxpayer to expand, exceed, or refine the common knowledge of skilled professionals within a scientific or engineering discipline, nor does it require the research project to succeed technically or commercially. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(4), a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on established principles of the physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to resolve technical uncertainty regarding the capability, method, or appropriate design of a new or improved business component. While the issuance of a utility or plant patent under 35 U.S.C. 151 serves as conclusive evidence under the regulatory patent safe harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) that the taxpayer discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty, a patent is not a precondition for claiming the credit. Conversely, design patents issued under 35 U.S.C. 171 are explicitly excluded from the regulatory safe harbor because they protect ornamental appearance rather than functional scientific or engineering innovation.

In federal audit examinations and judicial proceedings—exemplified by the Seventh Circuit's appellate ruling in Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15, and the U.S. Tax Court's decision in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (2024)—the Technological in Nature requirement operates inseparably from the Process of Experimentation test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and the Section 174 and Section 174A uncertainty threshold under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A). Performing basic engineering calculations on readily available data, complying with standard building codes, or conducting post-construction quality control tests fails to establish that at least 80% ("substantially all") of a business component's research activities constituted a systematic process of experimentation fundamentally relying on hard science principles. To satisfy 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), which requires taxpayers to retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit, corporate tax departments must link project-level Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) directly to specific hard science principles, documented initial uncertainties, and iterative evaluations of technical alternatives at the discrete business component or subcomponent level.
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Technological in Nature Mandate
Legislative Framework and Current Statutory Currency under IRC Section 41

Enacted originally in 1981 and made a permanent provision of the Internal Revenue Code by Section 121 of the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-113, Div. Q, Title I, § 121, enacted December 18, 2015, with § 121(a)(1) effective for amounts paid or incurred after December 31, 2014, and § 121(c)(1) effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2015), the IRC Section 41 credit operates as an activities-based tax incentive structured to stimulate domestic research and development. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), the regular research credit equals 20% of the excess of a taxpayer's qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over a statutory base amount. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1)–(3), QREs comprise the sum of in-house research expenses and contract research expenses. In-house research expenses are restricted to three specific statutory categories: employee wages paid or incurred for qualified services under § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), supplies used in the conduct of qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), and amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii). Contract research expenses generally equal 65% of amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any person other than an employee of the taxpayer for qualified research under § 41(b)(3)(A), increasing to 75% for amounts paid to a qualified research consortium under § 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for eligible energy research payments made to eligible small businesses, universities, or Federal laboratories under § 41(b)(3)(D).

To determine whether the underlying activities generating these expenditures constitute "qualified research," 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) establishes a mandatory Four-Part Test that must be applied separately with respect to each discrete business component of the taxpayer under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A). A business component is defined comprehensively under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. While secondary practitioner summaries frequently omit "invention" when listing eligible categories, the statutory text explicitly encompasses all six artifacts. Furthermore, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) establishes a special rule for production processes, mandating that any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component be treated as a separate business component distinct from the product being manufactured. This statutory bifurcation prevents routine manufacturing scale-up costs from being commingled with product design costs, while allowing genuine engineering experimentation on manufacturing machinery or plant processes to be evaluated on its own technical merits.

A foundational statutory update governs the threshold cross-reference in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A). Historically prior to 2022, and within the text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i), the provision referenced research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as expenses under section 174. During the mandatory capitalization and amortization period instituted by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) for taxable years beginning in 2022 through 2024, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) referenced research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174. Under current statutory law enacted on July 4, 2025, by Pub. L. 119-21 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), Congress enacted IRC § 174A to permanently reinstate immediate expensing for domestic research and experimental expenditures and amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to apply to research with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A. Consequently, the threshold eligibility inquiry under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) now links directly to domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A, while preserving the substantive regulatory standards of 26 CFR § 1.174-2.
Resolving Structural Ordering Conflicts in the Four-Part Test

A frequent source of analytical confusion in secondary tax commentary and practitioner literature involves the numbering, naming, and grouping of the Four-Part Test. Accounting firms and tax consultancies routinely reorganize the statutory requirements into pedagogical labels—such as "Permitted Purpose," "Elimination of Uncertainty," "Process of Experimentation," and "Technological in Nature"—and place Technological in Nature inconsistently as the second, third, or fourth element. This divergence occurs because practitioner frameworks frequently extract the regulatory definition of Section 174 uncertainty from 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and the qualified purpose definition from IRC § 41(d)(3) into standalone tests while merging the business component clause of IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) with the purpose rules.

Under the federal hierarchy of legal authority, the enacted statutory text of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and the final Treasury Regulations at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2) carry controlling legal weight over administrative guidance such as the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Audit Techniques Guide (ATG), which in turn supersedes secondary practitioner commentary. Both the statute at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A)–(C), the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (updated July 2, 2026), and the U.S. Tax Court in Little Sandy Coal (T.C. Memo. 2021-15) and Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113) structure the Four-Part Test in a precise statutory sequence. Understanding how practitioner pedagogical labels map onto the controlling statutory sequence is essential for preparing audit defenses and litigation briefs that align with judicial analysis.

cells: Test 1: Section 174 / Section 174A Test

Expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures in the experimental or laboratory sense, intended to discover information that eliminates uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design.

Establishes the initial technical unknown; under § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) and (a)(5)(i), the uncertainty must concern the development or improvement of a business component resolvable via hard science principles.
Frequently mapped as "Elimination of Uncertainty (Test 2)" in narrative guides or grouped with "Section 174 (Permitted Purpose)".
Test 2: Discovering Technological Information Test

Research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information which is technological in nature—meaning the process of experimentation fundamentally relies on physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.
Serves as the core scientific anchor (TIN), restricting eligible inquiry to the four enumerated hard science domains.
Often mapped as "Technological in Nature (Test 4)" in narrative summaries or "Part 3" in practitioner headers.
Test 3: Business Component Test

Application of the discovered technological information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention).
Requires that the technological information discovered be applied to a discrete, identifiable technical artifact or subcomponent under the shrinking-back rule.
Typically combined into "Permitted Purpose (Test 1)" in secondary practitioner commentary.
Test 4: Process of Experimentation Test

Substantially all (≥ 80%) of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation evaluating alternatives for a qualified purpose (function, performance, reliability, or quality; excluding style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design).
26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4) and (a)(5)(i) explicitly link TIN and POE: the evaluative process itself must fundamentally rely on hard science principles.
Commonly split between "Permitted Purpose (Test 1)" and "Process of Experimentation (Test 3)" in practitioner literature.

body.text: The Interlocking Mechanics of Uncertainty, Experimentation, and Hard Science Reliance

The Technological in Nature requirement does not function as an isolated statutory checkbox that can be satisfied merely by employing credentialed scientists or engineers. Instead, the regulation constructs a tight causal loop in which the Technological in Nature mandate governs the qualitative character of both the initial uncertainty encountered by the taxpayer and the evaluative methodology deployed to resolve that uncertainty. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information only if it is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component. Both 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i) define uncertainty in identical regulatory terms: uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component.

Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) explicitly embeds the Technological in Nature requirement into the four sequential elements required to establish a qualifying Process of Experimentation (POE). First, the taxpayer must identify initial technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component as of the beginning of the research activities. Crucially, the regulation stipulates that a taxpayer may undertake a qualifying process of experimentation even if there is no uncertainty regarding its capability or method of achieving the desired result, so long as the appropriate design of the desired result is uncertain at the outset. Second, the process of experimentation must fundamentally rely on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, the taxpayer must identify one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty and conduct an evaluative process—such as modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology—capable of evaluating those alternatives.

Fourth, the taxpayer must satisfy the quantitative 80% "substantially all" rule codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), which mandates that substantially all of the research activities with respect to the discrete business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)—namely, a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, while excluding activities related to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" threshold is satisfied only if 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose described in section 41(d)(3). When this 80% threshold is achieved, the remaining 20% or less of research activities conducted on that business component also qualify for the credit, provided those remaining activities independently satisfy the Section 174/174A test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and do not fall within the statutory exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4).

The structural integration of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4) and (a)(5)(i) produces a critical second-order audit consequence: an investigative activity can be highly uncertain, rigorously methodical, and empirically data-driven yet fail IRC Section 41 entirely if the underlying analytical domain is not a hard science. For instance, if an enterprise faces profound uncertainty regarding optimal organizational structure or consumer color preference and executes a sophisticated statistical regression across 5,000 focus-group respondents, the activity fails the Technological in Nature requirement because the methodology relies on behavioral psychology, marketing, and management science rather than physical, biological, engineering, or computer science. Conversely, if an engineering firm seeks to formulate a specialized concrete mixture capable of achieving a specific compressive strength alongside low thermal conductivity—where existing industry formulas cannot satisfy both physical parameters simultaneously—and executes systematic chemical ratio iterations, compressive stress testing, and thermal modeling, the activity satisfies the Technological in Nature requirement through its fundamental reliance on materials science, chemistry, and physical engineering.
The Four Pillars of Hard Science Reliance and Regulatory Safe Harbors

To substantiate that research activities are technological in nature under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), a taxpayer must demonstrate how its experimental methodology fundamentally relied on at least one of the four enumerated hard science domains, or establish conclusive qualification under the regulatory patent safe harbor.
Principles of the Physical Sciences

The physical sciences encompass disciplines that investigate non-living matter, energy, and chemical or physical transformations—principally physics, chemistry, materials science, thermodynamics, acoustics, optics, geology, and metallurgy. In an illustrative manufacturing scenario where a research team develops a biodegradable plastic bottle polymer engineered to decompose within 90 days without sacrificing shelf-life stability, the investigators synthesize varying chemical compound ratios, test molecular bond and tensile strength, and simulate environmental decay within controlled laboratory chambers. Because the underlying design uncertainty—whether polymer molecules can be structured to maintain tensile integrity during storage yet rapidly depolymerize under specific environmental triggers—is resolved through the application of polymer chemistry and materials physics, the process of experimentation is technological in nature. Notably, the IRS Audit Techniques Guide explicitly confirms that the analytical discipline governing the experimental process dictates qualification rather than the commercial sector or end user of the product: developing a novel chemical formulation for artists' paint relies fundamentally on chemistry and qualifies as technological in nature, even though the finished product is utilized strictly within the fine arts.
Principles of the Biological Sciences

The biological sciences encompass the study of living organisms and life processes, including biology, biochemistry, microbiology, genetics, pharmacology, botany, and food or agricultural sciences. Qualifying research activities within this domain include systematic experimentation to optimize microbial fermentation rates, assaying biochemical stability profiles across varying thermal or pH gradients, and conducting pre-clinical and clinical trials of pharmaceutical formulations. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv), clinical testing of pharmaceutical products conducted prior to full Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval—where a new functional use, characteristic, indication, combination, dosage, or delivery form requires regulatory approval—engages biological and pharmacological principles to resolve technical uncertainty and is not treated as excluded post-commercial-production activity.
Principles of Engineering

The engineering pillar encompasses mechanical, electrical, structural, civil, chemical, aerospace, and industrial engineering. Qualifying engineering activities involve applying physical and mathematical laws—such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD), finite element structural analysis (FEA), thermodynamic heat-transfer modeling, or iterative prototype stress testing—to resolve technical uncertainties in capability, manufacturing process method, or structural design. As illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4 Example 4, when an automobile manufacturer lowers a vehicle's hood to improve aerodynamic performance, thereby altering under-hood airflow and compromising engine cooling, the engineers' systematic evaluation of alternative hood geometries and cooling configurations relies fundamentally on aerodynamic and mechanical engineering principles.

Federal courts, however, enforce a rigorous boundary between experimental engineering and routine engineering calculation. In Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (decided December 23, 2024), a consulting engineering firm that designed mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) systems for building projects claimed IRC Section 41 credits. The U.S. Tax Court disallowed the credits in full, holding that complying with standard building codes and performing basic engineering calculations using already available data does not constitute an investigative process of experimentation because the taxpayer already possesses the information needed to determine the design. Similarly, in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, the Tax Court held that entering customer parameters into preexisting design spreadsheets whose output dictated the configuration of air pollution control equipment involved no technical uncertainty or scientific experimentation. Thus, employing licensed engineers to perform standard load, airflow, or sizing calculations without iterative hypothesis testing fails the combined Technological in Nature and Process of Experimentation requirements.
Principles of Computer Science

Computer science serves as the qualifying scientific foundation for software development, hardware architecture, firmware, and algorithmic engineering. Qualifying activities rely on principles of computational theory, data structures, algorithm design, compiler and operating system architecture, network protocols, cryptographic encryption, and database management systems—such as resolving architectural bottlenecks to reduce data processing latency below a critical millisecond threshold or engineering novel data compression algorithms. Conversely, routine software maintenance, standard configuration of commercially available off-the-shelf (COTS) software packages, or straightforward application programming interface (API) integration does not involve discovering technological information via computer science experimentation.

Furthermore, where computer software is developed by, or for the benefit of, the taxpayer primarily for internal use under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) (applicable in its current regulatory form to taxable years beginning on or after October 4, 2016), unless the software is developed for use in an activity that itself constitutes qualified research or a qualifying production process, the software must satisfy not only the standard Four-Part Test but also a stringent three-part High Threshold of Innovation Test. First, the internal-use software must be innovative, resulting in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable metric that is substantial and economically significant. Second, the software development must involve significant economic risk, where technical risk arises specifically from uncertainty that is technological in nature as defined in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), and substantial uncertainty must exist at the beginning of the taxpayer's activities under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C). Third, the software must not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer without modifications that would satisfy the first two requirements.
Abandonment of the Common Knowledge Discovery Test and Eligibility of Failed Projects

A pivotal regulatory milestone governing the Technological in Nature requirement is codified in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), promulgated in T.D. 9104 on January 2, 2004. Prior to T.D. 9104, earlier regulations issued in 2001 under T.D. 8930 had imposed a highly restrictive "Discovery Test" requiring taxpayers to prove that their research sought to obtain knowledge that exceeded, expanded, or refined the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the relevant scientific or engineering field. In response to legislative history and taxpayer comments, T.D. 9104 explicitly eliminated that requirement. Under currently operative 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(4), a determination that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature does not require the taxpayer to seek information that exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering in which the taxpayer is performing the research. Instead, a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and may rely on existing principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to satisfy this requirement under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), a legal standard reinforced by the Fifth Circuit in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009). Moreover, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) expressly provides that credit eligibility does not require that the taxpayer succeed in developing a new or improved business component.

A notable judicial anomaly arose in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, where the Tax Court's memorandum opinion erroneously cited the obsolete 2001 T.D. 8930 phrasing regarding exceeding, expanding, or refining common knowledge. Under the governing hierarchy of federal tax authority, the operative final regulation at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(4) as amended by T.D. 9104—alongside the IRS's own Audit Techniques Guide, which explicitly instructs examiners under Section 2.B that T.D. 9104 rejects the former requirement that research must obtain knowledge exceeding, expanding, or refining the common knowledge of skilled professionals in a particular field—controls over a nonprecedential Tax Court memorandum opinion's citation to superseded regulatory text. Furthermore, because both 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) divorce credit qualification from commercial or technical success, failed or abandoned research projects remain fully eligible for the IRC Section 41 credit, provided the failure or abandonment stemmed from unresolved technical uncertainties investigated through hard science experimentation rather than routine budget cuts or shifting consumer demand.
The Patent Safe Harbor under 26 CFR 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii)

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) establishes a specialized evidentiary safe harbor linking federal patent law to the Technological in Nature and uncertainty requirements. Under the exact text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), for purposes of section 41(d) and paragraph (a)(3)(i) of that section, the issuance of a patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 151—other than a patent for design issued under the provisions of 35 U.S.C. 171—is conclusive evidence that a taxpayer has discovered information that is technological in nature that is intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component, though the issuance of such a patent is not a precondition for credit availability.

Two critical legal boundaries govern the application of this safe harbor in audit practice. First, while secondary commentary frequently states broadly that any patent issued by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office triggers the conclusive presumption, the regulation applies solely to utility and plant patents issued under 35 U.S.C. 151 and expressly excludes design patents issued under 35 U.S.C. 171. Design patents are excluded because they protect ornamental appearance rather than functional technological innovation, aligning with IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), which bars credits for style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors. Second, as clarified in the Preamble to T.D. 9104, the patent safe harbor conclusively satisfies only the "discovering information that is technological in nature" and "elimination of uncertainty" requirements under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i). Holding a utility patent does not waive the separate statutory mandates requiring the taxpayer to satisfy the 80% Process of Experimentation test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6) and avoid the categorical exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4).
Demarcating Statutory Boundaries: Excluded Activities under IRC Section 41(d)(4)

To reinforce the Technological in Nature mandate and prevent non-scientific business expenditures from being claimed as qualified research, Congress enacted eight categorical exclusions in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H), amplified by 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(1)–(10). Even where a project involves technically trained personnel, expenditures attributable to excluded activities cannot be included in QREs.
The Social Sciences, Arts, and Humanities Exclusion under IRC 41(d)(4)(G) and 41(d)(4)(D)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(G) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8), qualified research explicitly excludes any research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities. In parallel, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(D)(i)–(v) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6) exclude efficiency surveys, activities relating to management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collection, and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control.

In contemporary enterprise product development, multi-disciplinary project teams frequently blend technical engineering with economic or behavioral modeling, creating severe audit exposure if hours are not rigorously segregated. For example, in developing a new financial technology (FinTech) platform, software engineers who design cryptographic security protocols, fault-tolerant distributed database architectures, or low-latency transaction matching engines rely fundamentally on principles of computer science under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4). Conversely, economists, actuaries, and compliance analysts assigned to the same project team who develop credit-scoring economic models, behavioral consumer nudges, or regulatory compliance workflows are engaged in economics, behavioral science, and management or legal support services excluded under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8) and (c)(6). Failing to segregate and exclude the social science and administrative hours contaminates the denominator of the 80% Process of Experimentation fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), risking the disqualification of the entire business component.
Adaptation and Duplication of Existing Business Components under IRC 41(d)(4)(B) and (C)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3), activities relating to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need do not constitute qualified research. Similarly, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) exclude duplication—defined as reproducing an existing business component in whole or in part from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information. Crucially, however, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) and (c)(4) contain vital limiting sentences: the adaptation exclusion does not apply merely because a business component is intended for a specific customer, and the duplication exclusion does not apply merely because the taxpayer examines an existing business component in the course of developing its own new or improved business component.

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10) and federal jurisprudence—including Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, and Davenport v. United States, 897 F. Supp. 2d 496 (N.D. Tex. 2012)—establish that the presence of genuine initial technical uncertainty is the dividing line between qualified custom engineering and excluded adaptation. Under Examples 3 and 6 of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10) and the holding in Betz, customizing an existing general ledger software platform to fit a customer's workflow (Example 3), reconfiguring a passenger rail car with fewer seats and different carpeting (Example 6), or delivering a copy of a prior wastewater treatment system modified only to meet published European site standards (Betz, M&W Ireland project) constitutes excluded adaptation because no fundamental technical uncertainty existed requiring scientific experimentation. Conversely, under Example 7 of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), where a valve manufacturer acquires preexisting robotic equipment to build an improved manufacturing process, encounters genuine technical uncertainty regarding how to modify the robotics to meet operational specifications, and conducts extensive laboratory and engineering tests to evaluate design alternatives, the activities are not excluded as adaptation.
Research After Commercial Production under IRC 41(d)(4)(A) and 26 CFR 1.41-4(c)(2)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i), any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of a business component is excluded from qualified research. Commercial production begins once the business component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer for the component's sale or use. Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(A)–(F) deems six specific operational activities to occur after commercial production has begun: preproduction planning for a finished business component, tooling-up for production, trial production runs, troubleshooting involving the detection of faults in production equipment or processes, accumulating data relating to production processes, and debugging flaws in a business component.

A nuanced doctrinal tension exists between the 1986 legislative history and the 2004 regulatory preamble regarding the interaction of IRC § 41(d)(4) exclusions and IRC § 41(d)(1). In the House Conference Report to the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (H.R. Conf. Rep. No. 99-841), Congress indicated that activities enumerated under IRC § 41(d)(4) are excluded without reference to whether they otherwise involve technological information or experimentation. In the Preamble to T.D. 9104 (2004), however, the Treasury Department and the IRS stated that the exclusions for research after commercial production, adaptation, and duplication do not exclude research activities that independently satisfy all requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1)—such as when a post-commercialization engineering effort addresses a new technical uncertainty to improve the component's performance or develops a separate manufacturing process under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii). Because federal courts (Betz, Eustace, Davenport) analyze IRC § 41(d)(4) exclusions independently of IRC § 41(d)(1) in adherence to the statutory phrase "Such term does not include any activity described in paragraph (4)," taxpayers must proactively isolate any post-production improvement or new manufacturing process as a separate business component or subcomponent under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to prevent it from being characterized as routine post-commercialization debugging or troubleshooting.
Additional Statutory Exclusions under IRC 41(d)(4)(F) and (H)

Completing the statutory framework of IRC § 41(d)(4), two additional exclusions restrict QRE eligibility regardless of the scientific rigor of the underlying work. First, under the Foreign Research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F), any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States is categorically excluded. Second, under the Funded Research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d), any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity is excluded unless the taxpayer both bears the financial risk of failure—meaning payment is contingent on the technical success of the research—and retains substantial rights in the resulting research.
Judicial Interpretation, the Substantially All Fraction, and IRS Audit Defense
The IRS Audit Techniques Guide Perspective on Technological Reliance

During an examination, IRS engineers and revenue agents evaluate research credit claims under the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Activities, updated July 2, 2026). While secondary commentary frequently asserts that IRS auditors scrutinize claims to verify whether taxpayers moved beyond reliance on "common knowledge," a rigorous reading of Section 2.B of the IRS ATG demonstrates a more precise administrative standard. The IRS ATG explicitly instructs examiners that under T.D. 9104, there is no requirement that the taxpayer obtain knowledge exceeding, expanding, or refining the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field. Instead, IRS examiners concentrate their audit scrutiny on two interlocking evidentiary thresholds: whether the information available to the taxpayer at the outset failed to establish capability, method, or appropriate design under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), and whether substantially all (≥ 80%) of the taxpayer's research activities on the business component constituted a structured process of experimentation that fundamentally relied on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)–(6).
Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner: Resolving the Tax Court and Seventh Circuit Conflict

The preeminent modern judicial precedent governing the intersection of engineering design, prototype fabrication, and the 80% Process of Experimentation fraction is Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner. Because the U.S. Tax Court (T.C. Memo. 2021-15, Dkt. No. 17431-17, decided February 11, 2021) and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit (62 F.4th 287, decided March 7, 2023) diverged sharply on a fundamental legal rule governing the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) 80% "substantially all" fraction while agreeing on the ultimate disallowance of the taxpayer's credit for failure of proof, distinguishing the two rulings is vital—with the Seventh Circuit's appellate opinion carrying controlling legal authority.

In Little Sandy Coal, the taxpayer's shipbuilding subsidiary, Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS), claimed IRC Section 41 credits for designing and building a customized tank barge (Project 720, for customer Apex Oil) and a floating dry dock (Project 730). Both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit agreed on three foundational legal principles regarding the relationship between engineering design, physical novelty, and scientific experimentation. First, CIS argued that it satisfied the 80% "substantially all" requirement because over 80% of the physical components of the vessels were new or redesigned; both courts rejected this contention, holding that under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the 80% test measures research activities, not the proportion of novel physical elements (expressly declining to follow broad language in Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010)), and that supply costs cannot be included in the activity fraction because supplies are tangible property rather than activities. Second, both courts held that building a "first-of-its-kind" vessel does not automatically establish that the taxpayer engaged in a scientific process of experimentation. Third, both courts held that post-construction testing that merely verifies a vessel functions as designed or satisfies contractual specifications—such as dry dock "raise-and-lower" tests or deadweight displacement surveys—constitutes excluded quality control testing under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(v) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) rather than a scientific process of experimentation evaluating technical alternatives.

Crucially, however, the Seventh Circuit (62 F.4th 287) explicitly overruled the Tax Court's legal reasoning regarding how direct support, direct supervision, and pilot model fabrication wages are treated in the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) 80% fraction. The Tax Court (T.C. Memo. 2021-15) had concluded that because IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) distinguishes between employees "engaging in qualified research" under clause (i) and employees "engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities" under clause (ii), production workers fabricating a pilot model or directly supporting research are by definition not engaged in research, meaning their activities could never be included in the numerator of the 80% process of experimentation fraction. Rejecting that categorical exclusion as a misreading of the statute and regulations, the Seventh Circuit established a three-part framework governing the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction.

body.text: Despite correcting the Tax Court's fraction rule in a taxpayer-favorable manner, the Seventh Circuit affirmed the judgment in favor of the IRS because CIS failed its evidentiary burden of proof: CIS maintained no project-level time records or technical documentation establishing what portion of its engineers' or production workers' activities constituted a scientific process of experimentation versus routine vessel fabrication, and arbitrary retrospective estimates could not cure the absence of a factual record. In subsequent litigation, Intermountain Electronics Inc. v. Commissioner, Tax Court Docket No. 11019-19, the Tax Court on April 9, 2024 denied an IRS motion for summary judgment that relied on Little Sandy Coal, holding that material facts remained in dispute regarding whether the taxpayer's pilot model production activities constituted a process of experimentation.
The Shrinking-Back Rule under 26 CFR 1.41-4(b)(2) and the Subcomponent Documentation Trap

When an overall product or system fails the Four-Part Test—most commonly because non-experimental engineering design, routine fabrication, or social science activities cause the overall business component to fall below the 80% Process of Experimentation threshold—26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) provides a vital salvage mechanism known as the shrinking-back rule. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), the requirements of section 41(d) and paragraph (a) of that section are to be applied first at the level of the discrete business component. If those requirements are not met at that level, then they apply at the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license. This shrinking back of the product is to continue until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and such element fails to satisfy the test.

In 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(3), the regulation illustrates this mechanism through a motorcycle engine builder that develops a new carburetor and modifies an existing engine design to accommodate it. If the modifications to the overall engine fail the Four-Part Test because less than 80% of the total engine activities involved experimentation, the inquiry shrinks back to the next most significant subset of elements—the new carburetor—allowing the research expenses attributable to developing the carburetor to qualify if the carburetor independently satisfies all four parts of the test, including Technological in Nature.

Recent federal and state decisions demonstrate, however, that the shrinking-back rule becomes an unworkable trap when taxpayers lack subcomponent-level cost accounting and technical documentation. In Little Sandy Coal (T.C. Memo. 2021-15 and 62 F.4th 287), the courts refused to apply the shrinking-back rule to specific vessel subcomponents—such as the tank barge's stern notch or towing bridle—because CIS tracked hours and costs solely at the overall vessel project level, leaving the court with no evidentiary basis to isolate subcomponent activities or calculate a subcomponent 80% fraction. Similarly, in Appeal of Abramson, et al. (California Office of Tax Appeals, 2024-OTA-635 issued December 14, 2023, and Opinion on Petition for Rehearing 2024-OTA-636 Nonprecedential issued October 9, 2024, OTA Case Nos. 21067893, 21118984, and 21119139), an architectural firm (Abramson Teiger Architects, LLP) contended that the tribunal erred by failing to apply 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2). The Office of Tax Appeals denied the claim, holding that vague timesheet entries—such as "design meeting" and "go through keynotes for plans"—and broad phase-level accounting failed to identify any specific subparts of business components or substantiate the exact time spent on sub-activities constituting a process of experimentation. Both the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal and the tribunal in Appeal of Abramson emphasized that estimating qualified wages is permissible only after the taxpayer has first established through specific, granular evidence that qualified research occurred on the discrete component or subcomponent.
Quantitative Worked Example: Computation of the 80% Substantially All Test, Shrinking-Back Rule, and QREs

To demonstrate how the Technological in Nature mandate under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), the 80% Process of Experimentation fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the Seventh Circuit's fraction rules in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), the shrinking-back rule under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), and the statutory QRE rates under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) interact mathematically, consider a domestic manufacturer, AeroTherm Corp., undertaking Project Horizon during Tax Year 2026 to develop a new industrial thermal-exchange unit (the Overall Business Component) consisting of three discrete subcomponents.

For Subcomponent A (Novel Ceramic-Matrix Composite Heat Core), engineers confront fundamental technical uncertainty at the outset regarding whether a new ceramic-matrix formulation can withstand thermal cycling at 1,100°C without micro-fracturing under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i); the team conducts systematic materials science and thermodynamic simulations, fabricates two iterative test cores (pilot models used strictly to test hypotheses and evaluate alternative compound ratios), and performs destructive stress testing under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)–(5). For Subcomponent B (Standard Steel Outer Casing & Mounting Frame), engineers perform routine computer-aided design (CAD) layout and basic load calculations using published structural steel tables and standard building codes (analogous to Phoenix Design Group, T.C. Memo. 2024-113), coupled with cosmetic exterior styling excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B); although 200 hours of initial concept exploration qualify as Section 174A research activities, zero hours involve a systematic process of experimentation evaluating uncertain technical alternatives. For Subcomponent C (Customer Market Feasibility & Pricing Study), marketing analysts and economists conduct customer preference surveys and economic elasticity modeling excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(iii) and § 41(d)(4)(G). AeroTherm Corp. tracks employee research hours and expenses cleanly at the subcomponent level as detailed in the table below.

body.text: In the first step of the mathematical verification, Subcomponent C is mandatorily excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D)(iii) and § 41(d)(4)(G) because it relies on economics and marketing rather than physical, biological, engineering, or computer sciences, failing the Technological in Nature test of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4). Consequently, all $45,000 of wages, $3,000 of supplies, and $10,000 of contract expenses attributable to Subcomponent C are eliminated from credit consideration.

In the second step, AeroTherm Corp. evaluates the overall thermal-exchange unit under the 80% "substantially all" rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6). If AeroTherm Corp. attempts to claim the thermal-exchange unit as a single overall business component encompassing all technical engineering hours across Subcomponents A and B (1,800 hours on Subcomponent A plus 800 hours on Subcomponent B, totaling 2,600 technical hours), the overall Process of Experimentation fraction is computed as:
Overall POE Fraction = 1,700 POE hours ÷ 2,600 total technical hours = 0.653846 (or 65.38%)

Because 65.38% falls below the 80.00% statutory threshold, the overall unit fails the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) "substantially all" requirement when routine casing design and code-compliance hours (Activity B2) are included in the denominator. Moreover, because Subcomponent B's 800 hours ($72,000 wages and $10,000 supplies) involved zero process of experimentation (0/800 = 0%), none of Subcomponent B's expenditures constitute eligible QREs.

In the third step, because AeroTherm Corp. maintained granular subcomponent-level documentation and time tracking, it applies the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate Subcomponent A (Ceramic-Matrix Composite Heat Core) as the discrete business component. Following the Seventh Circuit's holding in Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), the 500 hours of direct support pilot-core fabrication (Activity A2) are included in both the numerator and denominator because the test cores were fabricated and utilized as part of a methodical plan to test hypotheses and evaluate alternative ceramic formulations. The 100 hours of baseline literature and patent searches (Activity A3) constitute Section 174A research activities that are not themselves elements of a process of experimentation, so they are placed in the denominator only. In accordance with Little Sandy Coal (T.C. Memo. 2021-15), supply costs ($40,000) are excluded from the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) activity fraction. Computing the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) fraction for Subcomponent A by research hours and alternatively by employee wage cost yields:
Subcomponent A POE Fraction (Hours) = (1,200 hrs + 500 hrs) ÷ (1,200 hrs + 500 hrs + 100 hrs) = 1,700 hrs ÷ 1,800 hrs = 0.944444 (or 94.44%)

Under either measurement basis (94.44% by hours or 93.94% by wage cost), Subcomponent A exceeds the 80% ("substantially all") threshold. Furthermore, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), because at least 80% of Subcomponent A's research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, the remaining 20% or less of research activities on Subcomponent A (5.56% by hours or 6.06% by wage cost for Activity A3) also qualify because Activity A3 satisfies IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and is not excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4).

In the fourth step, AeroTherm Corp. computes its total Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b) for Subcomponent A. In-house qualified wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) equal $120,000 (A1) + $35,000 (A2) + $10,000 (A3) = $165,000. (To illustrate the separate 80% individual employee wage rule under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B): if Lead Materials Scientist Dr. Smith earned $150,000 in total annual W-2 taxable wages during 2026 and spent 1,700 of her 2,000 total annual work hours—1,700/2,000 = 85.00%—performing qualified services on Subcomponent A and 300 hours—15.00%—on general administrative tasks, 100% of her $150,000 annual W-2 wages would qualify because 85.00% meets the ≥ 80% "substantially all" individual employee threshold.) Assuming the table reflects the exact allocable qualified wages for the project team ($165,000), in-house supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) equal $15,000 (A1) + $25,000 (A2) = $40,000, and contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) at the 65% statutory rate equal $40,000 × 65% = $26,000. Strategic Implementation, Substantiation, and Form 6765 Compliance
Recordkeeping Mandate under 26 CFR 1.41-4(d) and Evolving IRS Disclosure Standards

To defend the Technological in Nature requirement during an IRS examination, taxpayers must comply with the recordkeeping mandate of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d). Under the exact text of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) (frequently misquoted in secondary practitioner literature using the plural "forms"), a taxpayer claiming a credit under section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit, cross-referencing the general record retention rules of 26 CFR § 1.6001-1 and authorizing the IRS and taxpayers to agree to guidelines for keeping specific records to substantiate research credits.

While the Preamble to T.D. 9104 confirms that the Treasury Department eliminated the separate "contemporaneous documentation requirement" that had briefly appeared in the 2001 T.D. 8930 regulations, contemporaneous technical records remain indispensable in practice because the taxpayer bears the entire legal burden of proving that every element of IRC § 41(d)(1) is satisfied. Furthermore, recent federal procedural rulings—including United States v. Harper, 847 Fed. App'x 408, and Premier Tech, Inc., No. 2:20-cv-890, enforcing the administrative specificity mandate of 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1)—alongside the IRS's administrative refund claim rules (IR-2021-203 effective January 10, 2022, updated on June 18, 2024 via FAQ 21) and the redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) have transformed R&D tax credit compliance from reactive back-end audit defense into mandatory upfront project-level disclosure.

When filing an amended return or refund claim for IRC Section 41 credits under the June 18, 2024 IRS administrative update, taxpayers must provide upfront three core categories of information: identification of all business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that year, a description of all research activities performed for each business component, and the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year. While the IRS waived the upfront submission of the fourth and fifth IR-2021-203 items—specifically, the names of individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover—effective June 18, 2024, the agency explicitly reserved the right to request those two items during an audit examination via an Information Document Request (IDR). In parallel, the redesigned Form 6765 requires granular business-component-level reporting structured around three core inquiries distilled from the Four-Part Test: the specific business component developed or improved by the taxpayer, the technical basis for qualification regarding uncertainty and experimentation, and the total cost allocated by QRE category.
Operationalizing Compliance: Technical Nexus Interviews and the Technical Nexus Matrix

To bridge the evidentiary gap between daily engineering execution and tax law substantiation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d), corporate tax departments should implement two structured internal compliance mechanisms alongside project-level cost accounting: Structured Technical Nexus Interviews (TNIs) and a standardized Technical Nexus Matrix.

Rather than relying on generic post-hoc narratives or ambiguous timesheet labels—which proved fatal to the taxpayers' claims in Little Sandy Coal and Appeal of Abramson—tax specialists should conduct formal, structured Technical Nexus Interviews with R&D and Engineering Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) during the tax year. Under the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, examiner interviews are explicitly designed to supplement and corroborate information obtained from reviewing existing records. Internal TNIs should therefore extract and cross-reference three specific evidentiary anchors: the exact baseline capability, method, or design parameters that were unknown at the outset of the project under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i); the specific principles of physical science, biological science, engineering, or computer science invoked under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4); and the specific design alternatives modeled, simulated, or tested through systematic experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i).

Complementing these contemporaneous interviews, taxpayers should maintain a Technical Nexus Matrix that links every claimed dollar of QREs across wages, supplies, leased computer time, and contract research to a qualifying hard science principle, a documented initial technical uncertainty, an evaluative process of experimentation, and contemporaneous engineering artifacts at the discrete business component or shrunk-back subcomponent level under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2).

body.text: Conclusion

The Technological in Nature requirement under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4) forms the structural linchpin of the federal R&D tax credit, ensuring that tax-subsidized research activities remain anchored in the physical sciences, biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. While Treasury Decision 9104 permanently eliminated the requirement that taxpayers expand or refine the common knowledge of skilled professionals and confirmed that technical or commercial failure does not bar qualification, federal appellate and Tax Court rulings—most notably Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), Phoenix Design Group (T.C. Memo. 2024-113), and Betz (T.C. Memo. 2023-84)—demonstrate that employing engineers or utilizing established scientific principles in routine design calculations, building code compliance, or customer adaptation fails the statute. Because 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)–(6) integrates hard science reliance directly into the 80% Process of Experimentation fraction, and because the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) cannot be invoked without granular subcomponent cost and time tracking, taxpayers must align their internal accounting and technical documentation with the business-component disclosure architecture of Form 6765 and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) to sustain IRC Section 41 credits upon examination.
